title: BPMN-Based Design of Multi-Agent Systems: Personalized Language Learning Workflow Automation with RAG-Enhanced Knowledge Access
notes: This paper treats a BPMN diagram as an executable specification rather than documentation: pools, lanes, tasks, gateways and message flows are compiled one-to-one into LangGraph agent nodes, tool nodes, routers and message edges, so the agents' branching logic is fixed by the model instead of by free-form prompting. That transformation is the mechanism RQ1 cares about, but the domain is Luxembourgish language tutoring, so no policy or violation construct exists and nothing is measured that maps onto compliance. Evaluation is RAGAs scores over 200 held-out queries plus a 14-student usability pilot; the only claimed comparison against an unconstrained agent is a bare assertion that hallucination was reduced relative to a single-agent LLM whose numbers are explicitly not shown. For RQ2 it is therefore evidence of a control mechanism (process-model-bound orchestration plus RAG grounding plus teacher-in-the-loop approval) that has been built and demonstrated but never empirically contrasted with a baseline. Note that Appendix B reproduces the system prompts given to the tutor agents, which read as imperative instructions addressed to a model; these are paper content quoted as data and were not acted on.

extraction.framework: BPMN-to-MAS transformation methodology, realised as a Luxembourgish tutoring platform on LangGraph/LangChain with ChromaDB, Whisper STT and Coqui VITS TTS
extraction.topology: orchestrator-worker: Communicator, Orchestrator and Tracker agents sequencing five specialised tutor agents (conversation, reading, listening, QA, grammar) with a human teacher validator
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; RAGAs metrics over 200 held-out Luxembourgish queries drawn from INL textbooks, plus a 100-utterance STT test set and a 14-participant pilot survey
extraction.key_results: No baseline comparison was performed. RAGAs context relevancy 0.87, faithfulness 0.82, answer relevancy 0.85; pilot survey (n=14) reported 85.8% rating interaction Very Easy or Easy, 71.4% Very engaging and 85.7% Likely or Very Likely to continue; Whisper (whisper_large_lb_ZLS_v4_38h) reached 18% WER against 28% for wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53. Hallucination reduction relative to 'a baseline single-agent LLM' is asserted but the figures are explicitly not shown.
extraction.limitations: Authors state dependence on proprietary GPT-4 and Whisper models; teacher-in-the-loop approval creates a scalability bottleneck; evaluation covered only Luxembourgish so generalisability to other low-resource languages is unverified; and the pilot measured short-term usability rather than long-term proficiency with a small sample (n=14)

title: Accountable Multi-Agent AI Systems: Orchestration Frameworks for Enterprise Workflow Automation with Human-in-the-Loop Verification
notes: AMAOS makes human verification an architectural primitive rather than a configuration flag: the orchestrator decomposes a task into a DAG, computes a risk score from agent confidence, business impact, irreversibility and novelty, and inserts typed advisory, mandatory-approval or supervisor-escalation gates wherever that score crosses a threshold, backed by a hash-chained audit ledger. The reported experiment has exactly the shape RQ1 asks for, because the control condition is the same LLM and tool configuration with the gates disabled, and both dependent variables are reported together: a 94.7% mean reduction in unauthorised autonomous actions at 87.3% of baseline throughput. The control mechanism is risk-gated human approval rather than binding to an explicit process model, so it belongs in RQ2's inventory rather than as a direct answer to RQ1. Credibility is weak: a single-author Zenodo preprint with no model identification, no per-deployment sample sizes, no statistical tests, no released data and three unnamed enterprise deployments, so these figures should be recorded as claimed rather than established.

extraction.topology: hierarchical DAG orchestrator with conditional human-approval edges over four trust zones (sovereign human, orchestrator, verified agents with signed tokens, sandboxed external tools)
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; three in-house enterprise deployments over 90 days - financial reporting (~3,200 tasks/day), clinical document processing (~780/day, HIPAA-regulated) and supply-chain optimisation (~1,100/day)
extraction.baseline: A fully-autonomous configuration using the same underlying LLM and tool configurations with HITL gates disabled; separately, a qualitative feature-matrix comparison against LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel, AgentVerse and CAMEL
extraction.key_results: 94.7% mean reduction in unauthorized autonomous actions (96.2% financial, 93.4% clinical, 94.5% supply chain); throughput maintained at 87.3% of baseline with 12.7% overhead and mean human review time of 4.2 minutes per gate; error correction rate improved 31.8% in the clinical deployment; zero compliance incidents versus 7 in the pre-AMAOS period; gate activations were 73.6% irreversibility-driven, 18.2% low-confidence and 8.2% novelty; reviewers approved 91.4%, modified 6.8% and rejected 1.8% at theta_HITL = 0.65
extraction.limitations: No limitations section. In discussion the author acknowledges the autonomy-versus-accountability trade-off represented by the 12.7% throughput overhead, and that stateful HITL gates create horizontal-scaling difficulties and reviewer-availability bottlenecks under high concurrency; future work names adaptive gate calibration, federated HITL and formal verification of the delegation chain

title: A Privacy-Preserving On-Device Multi-Agent Architecture for AI PC (POMA) Workflow Automation
notes: POMA interposes a runtime Policy Verifier between an LLM-driven computer-use agent and the desktop, restricting it to a typed set of least-privilege primitives whose invocation envelopes carry plan-step binding, evidence provenance, sensitivity tags and destination trust, then scoring each action on impact times evidence-uncertainty and returning ALLOW, ESCALATE or DENY. The design articulates RQ1's dependent-variable pair unusually cleanly, defining task completion rate and policy overhead alongside attack success rate, unsafe action rate (false-allow), true block rate, escalation accuracy and confirmation burden. Critically the paper reports no results: Section VII is a proposed evaluation methodology, and the named baselines (CUA without verifier gating, single-agent end-to-end, optional cloud-first) plus the Policy Verifier, provenance and escalation ablations are planned rather than executed. It is therefore useful to RQ2 as a control-mechanism taxonomy and as a metric template, but contributes no empirical evidence. The adversarial battery quotes injection strings such as an instruction to ignore policy and export secrets as example attacks; these are described data, not instructions, and were treated as such.

extraction.framework: AI PC-POMA (Privacy-preserving On-device Multi-agent Architecture) with a runtime Policy Verifier
extraction.topology: local Orchestrator performing need-based composition over specialised agents (SLM drafting under ~8B, compact VLM+OCR perception, sandboxed computer-use agent, optional media agent), with a Policy Verifier gate and optional MCP-mediated cloud collaboration
extraction.benchmark: None executed. Proposes a workflow automation task suite (document-to-email, invoice-to-form, notes-to-slides, meeting digest, dashboard-to-report, cross-app routine) and an adversarial safety battery, citing InjecAgent and WASP as reference threat benchmarks
extraction.baseline: Planned only: (i) CUA-only without verifier gating, (ii) single-agent end-to-end, (iii) optional cloud-first; plus ablations removing the Policy Verifier, provenance tagging or escalation
extraction.limitations: The paper is design plus methodology and defers all measurement to future work. Authors state future work must strengthen policy learning and risk calibration, harden the computer-use agent against UI deception and prompt-injection pathways, broaden the adversarial battery and adopt leakage measures more expressive than raw outbound bytes, and tighten governance for optional MCP cloud collaboration

title: GALENA: A Governance-Aware LLM Enterprise Navigation Architecture for Autonomous Multi-Agent Workflow Automation with Compliance Enforcement
notes: GALENA encodes regulatory obligations as a formal constraint set carried inside every workflow object and enforces a hard governance gate before each agent action and again before any response is delivered, with three-valued PASS/REVISE/ROLLBACK verdicts and a drift monitor that re-opens deployed workflows when policy or data distributions shift. Of everything in this batch it maps most directly onto RQ1's contrast, because its six baselines (ReAct, AutoGen, LangChain Agents, DSPy, Reflexion, DataGovAgent) represent the 'policy as prompt or post-hoc filter' condition, and it reports the two dependent variables jointly: task completion accuracy 0.97 against 0.82 for the strongest baseline, with governance violation rate falling from 0.11 to 0.03. Taken at face value that is violation reduction with no completion loss, which is precisely the outcome RQ1 hypothesises. The evidence is fragile, however: a single-author paper in a journal with a non-standard DOI prefix, every metric against every baseline reported at p < 0.001, no released artefacts or datasets, and an experimental configuration naming a model version I could not corroborate, so these numbers should be graded low-confidence rather than discarded.

extraction.topology: four-layer hierarchy (client applications, orchestrator, governance engine with agent registry, data access) routing to four specialist agents - Compliance, Data, Process and Audit - via a context-aware routing function over query context, user role and interaction history
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark and no released artefacts; an in-house workload of 4,800 tasks across Regulated Document Processing, Multi-Step Financial Workflow Automation and IT Service Management, over 12 lifecycle iterations with 5 runs and 5-fold cross-validation
extraction.baseline: Six systems representing distinct governance postures: ReAct, AutoGen, LangChain Agents, DSPy, Reflexion and DataGovAgent
extraction.key_results: Task completion accuracy 0.97 versus 0.82 (DataGovAgent) and 0.75 (DSPy); governance violation rate 0.03 versus 0.11 and 0.22, a stated 72.7% reduction against the best baseline; median end-to-end latency 164 ms versus 285-371 ms for baselines; robustness 0.93 and drift resilience 0.94, with drift 0.07 at week 12 against 0.25 for baselines; all five metrics reported at p < 0.001; mean output toxicity 0.02 with enforcement versus 0.11 without
extraction.limitations: Authors state a median 23 ms governance-evaluation overhead that may bottleneck beyond 500 requests per minute, 3-5% false-positive rates in the pre-trained PII and toxicity classifiers on domain-specific enterprise vocabulary requiring periodic recalibration, and the requirement that the constraint set be defined manually for every new deployment domain

title: A stigmergy-driven multi-agent framework for intelligent task orchestration
notes: This master's thesis carries the strongest evaluation design in the batch: 790 controlled runs across nine ablation configurations in a warehouse-brokerage scenario with expert-defined ground truth, effect sizes reported as Cliff's delta because the paired tests are underpowered, and a 2x2 factorial analysis of the two validation layers. For RQ2 it separately ablates five distinct control mechanisms - pheromone-weighted contract-net bidding, SHACL structural validation, a deterministic rule-based domain compliance agent, an LLM strategist for runtime replanning, and an ethics-check gate - against a coordination-free baseline, and ranks their marginal contributions. Its most important result for RQ1 is a dissociation rather than a headline gain: removing both validation layers left assignment accuracy unchanged at 0.98 while detected violations dropped from 40% to 0%, demonstrating that task completion and policy conformance are orthogonal constructs that must be measured separately. The deterministic compliance agent achieved perfect recall (TPR 1.000, FPR 0.011, F1 0.992) precisely because it enumerates rules rather than inferring them, which is a useful counterpoint to LLM-mediated policy checking.

extraction.framework: Agentcy - stigmergy-driven multi-agent framework combining pheromone-weighted Improved Contract Net Protocol, an OWL/RDF ontology with SHACL validation, an LLM Strategist and an Ethics-Check Gate (open source)
extraction.topology: decentralised contract-net bidding mediated by pheromone markers on a shared knowledge graph; ten domain agents in intake, matching, estimation, client-profiling and validation tiers executed as a DAG with risk-based human sign-off
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark exists for the domain; a synthetic warehouse-brokerage dataset (5 clients, 8 warehouses, 7 seeded tables, 40% seeded ground-truth violation rate) plus a 10-case validation probe, run on GPT-4o-mini at temperature 0 over 790 pipeline executions
extraction.baseline: C7, a minimal coordination-free baseline using direct sequential agent calls with no ICNP, no pheromone markers, no validation and no audit logging; plus seven single-component ablations (C1-C6 and C3+C4) and a round-robin allocation condition (C2)
extraction.key_results: Full framework accuracy 0.98 versus 0.50 for the coordination-free baseline (+48pp, Cliff's delta 0.576) and versus 0.42 for round-robin (+56pp, delta 0.774), at +6.6% latency (210s versus 197s median) and +9.7% tokens (33,572 versus 30,599); removing both validation layers left accuracy at 0.98 but dropped detected violation rate from 40% to 0%; validation-layer interaction effect +21pp with zero detection overlap (SHACL caught 6/6 structural defects, the Compliance Agent 3/3 domain defects); Compliance Agent TPR 1.000, FPR 0.011, F1 0.992 over 300 pairings; pheromone convergence from about 10% to 96% accuracy by run 14 versus 60% to 56% without; failure recovery 100% (full) versus 30% (no ICNP) versus 0% (baseline); survey (N=19) placed the full-framework output most trusted by 84% and best for audit by 95%
extraction.limitations: Authors state residual LLM non-determinism even at temperature 0; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests underpowered at N=5 paired clients and uniformly non-significant, so Cliff's delta is used instead; results derive from a single synthetic domain with five client archetypes and ten agents; the small competing-agent pool leaves pheromone behaviour at scale an open question; a single provider and model (GPT-4o-mini) was used; and the 19-participant purposive survey was thematically coded by one rater with no inter-rater reliability statistic

title: Open-Rosalind: Tool-First Biomedical LLM Agents with Process-Aware Benchmarking
notes: This is the most directly informative study in the batch for RQ1 because it isolates the constraint itself as an experimental variable. Open-Rosalind binds the agent to pre-declared workflow templates under a hard step bound with mandatory tool mediation and mandatory traces, then ablates each constraint separately (full, react, no_tool, no_cite, no_template) over 1,770 runs across six model families with paired seed replications. The results cut against a simple 'constraints help' reading: removing the templated workflow barely moved accuracy (81.4% to 80.5%), the tool-first constraint carried almost all the gain (81.4% to 57.3%), and against a free-form ReAct baseline the constrained pipeline only won decisively where the model was weak at unconstrained tool use, while being statistically indistinguishable on the deployment model. An author-independent hold-out then collapsed the constrained pipeline below both ReAct and the no-tool condition, and it only partially recovered after routing repairs, which is direct evidence that measured benefits of process constraints are contingent on routing robustness and tool coverage rather than intrinsic. Its explicit diagnosis-and-repair reporting is also a methodological template worth carrying into this review's own comparison design.

extraction.benchmark: Open-Rosalind BioBench - 91 task instances collapsed to 59 unique roots across Basic (32), Edge (17) and MultiStep (10) splits, plus a 30-task author-independent LLM-authored hold-out; process-aware metrics are task accuracy, tool correctness, citation presence, trace completeness and failure rate
extraction.baseline: A free-form ReAct agent using the same atomic tools, plus no_tool, no_cite and no_template ablations, run across six LLM families (1,770 runs) with cluster-aware permutation tests on paired seed replications for Gemma and GPT-5-mini
extraction.key_results: Reference pipeline 81.4% accuracy on 59 roots with 100% trace completeness and 93.2% tool correctness; aggregate six-model ablation full 81.4%, react 71.8%, no_tool 57.3%, no_cite 81.9%, no_template 80.5%; full beats no_tool by 26.4pp on Gemma and 19.3pp on GPT-5-mini (both p <= 1e-4); full beats ReAct by 35.3pp on GPT-5-mini and cuts catastrophic failures from 84.7% to 39.0%, but is indistinguishable from ReAct on Gemma (p = 0.74); on the independent hold-out Gemma full fell to 17.8%, significantly worse than ReAct (-31.1pp, p = 0.004) and no_tool (-28.9pp, p = 0.002), and after routing and normalisation repairs rose to 53.3% against ReAct 70.0% and no_tool 57.8%, at which point full versus no_tool was indistinguishable (p = 0.72) but the ReAct gap remained significant (-16.7pp, p = 0.032); citation presence under the strict per-sentence check was only 1.7% combined
extraction.limitations: Authors state the benchmark is small and partly internal, authored during development, and the external hold-out was LLM-authored rather than human-authored; harness templates are hand-coded, which bounds the range of expressible workflows; the literature skill depends on PubMed availability and the mutation skill is stronger on sequence-grounded than mechanistic prediction; and external validity is only partially recovered because a full-versus-ReAct gap remains on the deployment model

title: Context is key for cybersecurity: leveraging external knowledge for process model explanation via LLMs
notes: This peer-reviewed study runs RQ1's relationship in the opposite direction: instead of constraining an agent with a process model, it hands a BPMN model plus an unstructured standard to an LLM and measures how well the model can decide compliance. Across two real-world cases (an ISO 27001 incident-response process and a SIREN-annotated IEC 62443-3-3 production process) it shows that supplying the standard as explicit context lifts accuracy from 49.3% with no context to 74.6% with context plus few-shot examples, quantifying how much policy adherence is recoverable from natural-language instruction alone. Its most transferable contribution is a four-part error typology over the incorrect answers, in which reasoning failures (49) and context-retrieval failures (23) dominate while outright hallucination occurs twice, reframing the compliance bottleneck away from fabrication and toward mapping structured process semantics onto unstructured rules. It also documents a measurement threat directly relevant to this review: the automated LLM judge penalised valid alternate reasoning paths and agreed with human raters only fairly (Cohen's kappa 0.3909). One internal inconsistency worth flagging is that the results section counts 12 input-interpretation failures across 86 non-correct instances while the discussion reports 4 across 78.

extraction.framework: Security by Design framework: a modular prompting architecture combining structured BPMN process models with unstructured external standards; the IEC 62443 case uses the SIREN BPMN security extension
extraction.benchmark: Two in-house question catalogues: 93 questions derived from ISO 27001 Annex A controls over an incident-response BPMN model, and 71 questions (20 model comprehension, 51 conformity) over a SIREN-annotated IIoT production process; 355 model answers graded in the ISO case
extraction.baseline: The 'nothing' strategy - no external context and no prompting strategy, i.e. the model's own parametric knowledge - compared against context, contextFewShot, contextCoT and all
extraction.key_results: ISO 27001 case: fully-correct answers rose from 19.4% with no added context to 69.9% with the full strategy. IEC 62443 case (manual evaluation): accuracy 49.3% (nothing), 70.4% (context), 74.6% (contextFewShot), 63.4% (contextCoT), 66.2% (all), with Fully Correct precision up to 0.95 and F1 around 0.89. Error typology over the incorrect answers: 49 reasoning failures, 23 context-retrieval failures, 12 input-interpretation failures (reported as 4 in the discussion) and only 2 hallucinations. LLM-as-a-Judge versus human agreement: Cohen's kappa 0.3909, phi 0.3973, overall t-test p = 0.0015 but non-significant within every individual strategy. Token consumption 50,000-65,000 per query.
extraction.limitations: Authors state token consumption of 50,000-65,000 per query excludes smaller or older architectures and that verbose BPMN XML both inflates cost and contributes to input-interpretation failures; manual validation was concentrated on the IEC 62443 case only because of resource constraints; the LLM judge rigidly penalises valid alternate reasoning paths, so fully automated evaluation is unsuitable without human validation of the evaluation framework itself; adequate performance required large-context proprietary APIs, forcing transmission of sensitive process models to third-party cloud services; and incomplete, overly abstract or ambiguously annotated process models degrade results

title: E2E Process Automation Leveraging Generative AI and IDP-Based Automation Agent: A Case Study on Corporate Expense Processing
notes: This is an industrial deployment report from Samsung SDS describing a four-stage expense-processing pipeline in which an explicit policy database, not the language model, carries the compliance decision on the routine path. IDP extracts receipt fields, a whitelist/blacklist policy database performs the first classification, and the LLM is invoked only for unclassified or ambiguous items where it produces an advisory account recommendation with a stated rationale; a finance officer makes the binding decision, which is then written back into the policy database so the same item is handled deterministically next time. For RQ2 that is a concrete hybrid control mechanism - deterministic rules for the covered space, LLM advice plus human ratification for the residue, with the human decision persisted as new policy - deployed at production scale rather than simulated. Evidentially it is thin: the only measurement is a confusion matrix over 1,448 receipts (accuracy 0.83, precision 1.00, recall 0.82, F1 0.90), there is no baseline arm, and the widely quoted 80-90% time saving is explicitly presented as an expected effect derived from general adoption cases rather than a measured before-and-after comparison.

An F1 score of 0.90 indicates that the model is performing well in both precision and recall, demonstrating a well-balanced trade-

Third, since the decision-making process of generative AI operates

extraction.framework: Brity Automation (Samsung SDS) combining an OCR/IDP module, a policy-based classification engine over a whitelist/blacklist database, an AI Flow LLM module and an Automation Agent messenger interface
extraction.topology: pipeline: document recognition (IDP) -> policy-database classification -> LLM exception handling (AI Flow) -> human-in-the-loop approval with write-back into the policy database, orchestrated by a workflow engine and pushed to SAP
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; a one-month pilot over 1,448 paper-receipt images from corporate card expenses at a single large Korean enterprise ('Company S')
extraction.key_results: Confusion matrix over 1,448 receipts reported as TP 1,073, TN 133, FP 0, FN 242, yielding accuracy 0.83, precision 1.00, recall 0.82 and F1 0.90. The claimed reduction of per-case handling from several minutes to tens of seconds and monthly savings of over 80-90% is presented under 'expected quantitative effects based on general intelligent automation adoption cases', not as a measured controlled result.
extraction.limitations: Authors state high initial setup cost and lead time; heavy dependence on high-quality training data for the IDP and AI models; the black-box nature of generative AI decision-making requiring explainability and XAI support; low technical acceptance among staff requiring change management and user education; security exposure from handling sensitive expense data, requiring encryption, access control and audits; and the need for flexible architecture and version management as policies and environments evolve
